title: On Justice: A Short Philosophy
author: Justin Addam Higgins
desc: A complete original philosophy book on justice: the question, three rival views with objections, a thought experiment, and an open conclusion. Written to be read slowly. Worked against the real case of Based on JAH-SPEC-395086.

chapters.b:
Everyone uses the word 'justice', but few stop to ask what it means.

This book is a slow walk around justice: looking at it from several sides, testing each view, and leaving you with better questions than you started with.

We begin with the ordinary sense of 'justice' — how the word works in daily life — because philosophy that cannot touch ordinary life is only decoration. We will test our ideas against a real case along the way: Based on JAH-SPEC-395086.

The Mystic'S View holds that justice is best understood through what it does for us.

Its strongest argument: it makes sense of our feelings about justice.

Its hardest objection: it proves too much — or too little.

Hold both the argument and the objection in mind. justice deserves that much patience.

The Practical View holds that justice is best understood through careful reasoning.

Its strongest argument: it fits what we actually do and say.

Its hardest objection: ordinary people find it hard to live by.

Hold both the argument and the objection in mind. justice deserves that much patience.

The Modern View holds that justice is best understood through careful reasoning.

Its strongest argument: it fits what we actually do and say.

Its hardest objection: it seems to miss something essential about justice.

Hold both the argument and the objection in mind. justice deserves that much patience.

Imagine two worlds, identical except in one detail about justice.

In the first world, the ordinary view is exactly right. In the second, the skeptic is right.

Now ask: what would be different for the people living there? What would they do differently?

If nothing changes, perhaps the dispute about justice is only words. If everything changes, you have found what is really at stake.

Thought experiments do not settle questions; they show you where the question lives.

We have circled justice from 3 sides and found no single view without cost.

That is not failure. Philosophy rarely ends with a trophy; it ends with clearer sight.

Carry these questions into your week and watch how justice shows up in small decisions.

The unexamined idea is not worth much — but the examined one is worth everything.

A last exercise: take Based on JAH-SPEC-395086 and ask which of the three views it supports — then steelman the view it seems to refute.
